newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Federal Reserve leaves key rates unchanged.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Federal Reserve leaves key rates unchanged.

text.p: The U.S. Federal Reserve opted on Wednesday to hold interest rates steady amid signs that the economy is on course for modest growth with stable inflation next year.

The decision by the central bank's policy-making Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) had been widely expected and left the key federal funds and discount rates unchanged. The funds rate, which commercial banks charge each other for overnight money, remains a 5.25 percent and the discount rate, which the Fed charges member banks for cash, stays at 5 percent.
"The Federal Open Market Committee meeting ended at 12:25 p.m. (1725 GMT). There is no further announcement," central bank spokesman Joseph Coyne said in a brief statement.

After sprinting ahead at a 4.7 percent annual clip in the second quarter, the economy slowed to a 2.2 percent growth rate in the third -- a pace that most analysts reckon is sustainable on a long-term basis without fanning inflation.
Curbing inflation is considered critical to prolonging the economic expansion that began in March 1991 and now is in its sixth year without showing signs of serious flagging.

A "Blue Chip" survey of about 50 top private economists released this week found that on average they expect the economy to grow by 2.2 percent in 1997 after expanding by 2.4 percent this year. Consumer prices were seen rising by three percent in 1997, after increasing by 2.9 percent this year.
The Labor Department said Wednesday that producer prices rose at their fastest clip in seven months in October, jumping by 0.4 percent after a 0.2 percent increase in September.
But the rise was totally due to surging prices for food and energy. After stripping out those volatile costs, producer prices actually fell last month, by 0.3 percent.
"There's not a lot of inflation," said Sally Kleinman, senior economist at Wall Street broker Chase Securities.

That is good news for the financial markets. Stock and bond prices have surged in recent days on the benign economic outlook, although both markets gave up a bit of those gains on Wednesday as investors cashed in some of their profits.
Only seven weeks ago many Wall Street firms were arguing that the Fed needed to tighten credit to cool off an economy that seemed to be on the verge of over-heating.

But the slowdown in the economy since then has taken the pressure off the central bank to act to restrain growth. Most analysts expect it to decide again to hold rates steady at its last policy-making meeting of the year on Dec. 17.
But that does not mean that the central bank is about to let down its guard against inflation.
At 5.2 percent, the unemployment rate is hovering around a 7-1/2-year low and is at a level that in the past has presaged stepped-up wage demands from workers, and higher inflation.
That is why some analysts believe the Fed secretly decided Wednesday to continue to lean in the direction of higher interest rates by adopting an "asymmetrical" policy directive.
That would mean it would be predisposed to increasing rates if necessary to contain inflation.
Many analysts believe that it will indeed need to raise rates next year to keep inflation in check and the economy on course for continued expansion.
"The Fed will have to begin tightening by the spring," said James Glassman, an economist at Chemical Securities on Wall Street.

The central bank has not changed rates since January when it trimmed both the federal funds and discount rates by a quarter percentage point to help the economy through what Chairman Alan Greenspan called "a soft patch."
